newsitem.title: USA: NY Fed's Fisher ties stable dollar, U.S. growth.
newsitem.headline: NY Fed's Fisher ties stable dollar, U.S. growth.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of New York executive vice president Peter Fisher, on Thursday, tied the recent stability of the U.S. dollar to the good performance of the U.S. economy.

"The U.S. economic performance has been awfully good," Fisher told reporters as he presented the New York Fed's quarterly report on Treasury and Federal Reserve Foreign Exchange Operations prepared for Congress.
The report showed the dollar virtually unchanged against the mark and other major currencies in the third quarter.
The dollar's main move during that period was a 1.6-percent appreciation versus the yen.

"The macroeconomic conditions that exist today in the U.S. are so much better than foreign exchange market participants were forecasting two or three years ago..." said Fisher who added that the foreign exchange market is "surprised" at the non-fulfillment of its past predictions of a declining dollar.
Fisher also noted that U.S. monetary authorities did not intervene during the third quarter for the fourth consecutive quarter -- the longest stretch since April 1981-June 1982.
However, Fisher cautioned against concluding that the absence of intervention means U.S. monetary authorities want the dollar to remain at current levels.
"It would be a mistake to try to draw an inference from this (absence of intervention)," Fisher said.
"We believe in the floating rate regime," he stated.

Volatility during the third quarter was essentially limited to one day -- July 16 -- when the dollar traded within a 3.1-percent range versus the mark as the U.S. equity market underwent a sharp decline.
Fisher said that the Treasury and the Fed decided to "pause and see whether it was temporary" before intervening. He stressed that the Fed "never focuses on one-day market prices."

Fisher, who also is the Federal Open Market Committee's manager for the system open-market account, described the July 16 dollar fluctuation as "a very abrupt move that looked like position liquidation in a thin market on a day when there were sharp moves in the equity market."

Answering a question about foreign exchange models and dollar forecasts, Fisher responded "I don't know anyone who has a model of foreign exchange determination that can take them to the third digit."
"That's one reason why we believe in the floating rate regime," he added.
Fisher also stressed that interest rate differentials are "an important component," but only one among many others, that determine foreign exchange rates.
